problem_statement: The paper frames dynamic portfolio optimization as choosing the best trading trajectory for a portfolio of assets over time, while accounting for transaction costs and other constraints. It presents this as a central problem in quantitative finance.
problem_statement_quotes: In this paper we tackle the problem of dynamic portfolio optimization, i.e., determining the optimal trading trajectory for an investment portfolio of assets over a period of time, taking into account transaction costs and other possible constraints. This problem is central to quantitative ﬁnance.
In quantitative ﬁnance, portfolio optimization is the problem of selecting the best distribution of assets that optimizes some objective function [1].
The dynamic problem is more complex because transactions’ costs and transactions’ market impact must be taken into account, as well as other possible constraints.
classical_baseline: The paper benchmarks against classical solvers, specifically Gekko and an exhaustive brute-force solver. It also contrasts the discrete industry formulation with the continuous formulation, which it says can be solved exactly when transaction costs are absent.
classical_baseline_quotes: We benchmark our algorithms using two classical methods: a Gekko solver (a Python-based optimization suite [13]) and an exhaustive solver.
The classical methods were implemented as a benchmark of the rest of the algorithms.
When no transaction costs are present, the problem can actually be solved exactly.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the dynamic version is more complex because transaction costs, market impact, and other constraints must be included, and that the problem is intractable for generic instances. It also states that the discrete formulation maps to an Ising spin glass that is NP-hard in the generic case.
classical_difficulty_quotes: The dynamic problem is more complex because transactions’ costs and transactions’ market impact must be taken into account, as well as other possible constraints.
In practice, it is well-known that this is an intractable problem for generic instances.
Ising spin-glasses are known to be NP-Hard in the generic case [16], demonstrating that the portfolio optimization problem can be computationally costly.
business_stakes: The paper emphasizes that transaction costs can be comparable to portfolio profit, and that the problem is relevant to big industry players and investment funds that trade in large, discrete amounts. It also notes that market impact and the 10-5-40 rule are commercially relevant constraints.
business_stakes_quotes: These frequently are comparable to the proﬁt incurred by a given portfolio.

In this article, we chose to discuss the portfolio optimization problem with discrete variables, which is more relevant to big industry players, as investment funds typically trade in large, discrete amounts.
There exist many commercially relevant variations of this problem.
It is common for investors to be bound by a constraint known as the 10 −5 −40 rule
extraction_notes: motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; paper also discusses commercially relevant constraints
